summary:
Earth System Trend Detective helps renewable energy providers see how the climate conditions behind their projects are changing, region by region, using NASA data. The user picks a region and a variable, and the tool plots the monthly time series and reports the change per decade, a 95% range, a p-value and a plain-language verdict on whether the change is statistically significant.

Solar, wind and hydro “lenses” turn each result into a one-sentence takeaway for energy planning: temperature and aerosol trends for solar, 50 m wind-speed change for wind, and precipitation, runoff, evaporation and snow trends for hydro. The statistics use Sen’s slope and the Mann-Kendall test with a Hamed-Rao autocorrelation correction, which cut false alarms from 31% to 7% on simulated trend-free data. The tool declines to give a verdict when the data are unreliable, such as snow in regions with almost none.

Demo regions: US Southwest (solar), Great Plains (wind) and Pacific Northwest (hydro), plus a farming demo in California’s Central Valley. It runs offline from a fresh clone. It is long-term regional screening only, not a substitute for site measurements.
details:
Earth System Trend Detective is a free online tool that shows how NASA’s Earth science data has changed over time for a selected area. It also checks whether these changes are statistically meaningful or just natural variations. This tool is designed for students and the general public, with each variable explained in simple terms.

WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

We use NASA’s monthly data from 2000 onward, including MERRA-2 (temperature, wind, aerosols, sunlight, cloud cover), GPM IMERG (precipitation), and GLDAS (soil moisture, evaporation, snow). For any chosen region, the tool averages the data across the area, can remove seasonal patterns if you want, and calculates the rate of change per decade. This includes a 95% confidence range and a statistical test that accounts for monthly data connections. For the contiguous US, we also prepared trend maps for every grid cell, with corrections to avoid wrongly flagging thousands of cells as significant. Cells that are not significant appear faded, and we explain that “not significant” doesn’t mean “no change.” For example, the US Southwest has warmed about 0.5 °C per decade, which is statistically significant, while precipitation across the US shows almost no significant change.

WAYS TO UNDERSTAND THE RESULTS

Each result can be viewed through lenses like solar energy, wind energy, hydropower, or farming. These come with carefully written explanations that highlight the findings as long-term regional trends are not replacements for site-specific measurements. Results that are less reliable like sparse snow data don’t get these lens explanations.

BENEFITS AND PURPOSE

The tool makes NASA data and basic climate statistics easy to understand. It helps build data literacy by clearly showing uncertainty and gives renewable energy planners and farmers a quick initial look at long-term regional changes before they do more detailed analyses.

WHAT MAKES IT UNIQUE

A friendly animated fox named Comet guides users through interactive tutorials. You can explore the same data on a 3D globe, a terrain map with elevation lines, or a simple classic view. We purposely show results that aren’t statistically significant, highlight known data issues (such as some soil moisture maps and the fact that wind speed from monthly averages can underestimate real wind), and avoid tweaking regions or time periods just to find significance.

TECHNOLOGY USED

The backend is built with Python (FastAPI, xarray, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, pymannkendall) and accesses NASA Earthdata and GES DISC via earthaccess. The frontend uses JavaScript with Plotly for charts and CesiumJS for the 3D globe and terrain. Boundaries come from Natural Earth. The app is hosted on Vercel with code available on GitHub. Data processing was done on a desktop PC, and development occurred on a laptop. AI tools like Claude Code (coding), Google Stitch (UI design), and Google Gemini (guide artwork) assisted development. All results come from NASA data and the app’s own statistical methods.

THINGS WE TOOK INTO ACCOUNT

We focused on honest statistics (considering data connections, multiple tests, and reliability flags), data limits, making it accessible to non-experts, ensuring a demo that works with slow internet (by using small precomputed data and locally stored libraries), giving proper credit for data and map sources, and clearly stating what the results can and cannot say.

Live demo: https://nasa-app-challenge-lilac.vercel.app
